action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait, distractibility and entrainment; witnessed events with forced eye closure and side-to-side head movements
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe an event
action_criteria.rationale: Six weeks of right leg weakness and shaking episodes: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as the Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and entrainment and on the semiology of observed events, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: He has two to four shaking episodes a day, fears epilepsy, and a maternal aunt has epilepsy. Recording his habitual events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and assesses co-occurring epilepsy, as the AAN guideline advises. Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No lesion explaining the right leg weakness
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: He fears multiple sclerosis and the outside CT was normal; preserved reflexes, flexor plantars, intact posterior column sensation and the positive signs already answer the structural question, so a single non-contrast scan is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: As-needed lorazepam identified as a benzodiazepine not to be used for the events; antidepressant warning under 25 years
action_criteria.label: Review the current medicines, including the as-needed lorazepam
action_criteria.rationale: He takes lorazepam as needed; benzodiazepine rescue for the events would reinforce an epileptic model and sedate. At 22 the sertraline age warning also applies while his PTSD and depression are treated.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify his post-traumatic, mood and anxiety symptoms to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only, with no bearing on this patient's work-up
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Reading on positive signs and treatment trials is background knowledge, not a clinical step; nothing in this patient's diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat CT after the normal outside scan, repeat MRI, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional right leg weakness and functional seizures) based on the right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait, distractibility and entrainment, and on the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information. Address his fear of multiple sclerosis or epilepsy with the positive signs and the features of the events, without insisting that stress caused the symptoms.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).

Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder after witnessing the fatal accident (trauma-focused therapy), with his depression and anxiety.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Do not use his as-needed lorazepam to abort the events; review it with his prescriber and taper it gradually as his anxiety treatment allows.

avoided_actions.rationale: He has no syncope, palpitations or chest pain, and the events are shaking with retained responsiveness; an ECG adds nothing.
No murmur, syncope or embolic question is raised; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
He answers questions throughout the shaking and has no syncope or palpitations; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
A head CT at the outside emergency department three weeks ago was unremarkable; repeating it answers no new question and adds radiation.
He is afebrile with no inflammatory or encephalopathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add iatrogenic risk and feed his fear of multiple sclerosis without a question to answer.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in functional seizures or functional weakness and answers no question in this patient.

The right leg weakness has normal reflexes, tone and bulk with a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness; it is not neuromuscular, and a normal EMG would only feed the search for an organic cause.
Sensory loss of the right leg and lower abdomen splitting at the midline, with intact vibration and proprioception, is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with weakness and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Several shaking episodes a day, his own fear of epilepsy and a maternal aunt with epilepsy. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

differential.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis or another structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Progressive right leg weakness with sensory loss reaching the lower abdomen, and his fear of multiple sclerosis, raise demyelination or a cord lesion; symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, normal tone, normal bladder function, intact vibration and proprioception, and a positive Hoover sign with collapsing weakness are incompatible with a corticospinal, dorsal column or hemicord lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: The right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait, distractibility and entrainment of the event shaking are validated rule-in signs; the midline-splitting sensory loss and Romberg sway are supportive only.

The witnessed events had forced eye closure, asynchronous shaking of varying frequency, side-to-side head movements and retained responsiveness, and two habitual events were recorded on video-EEG without ictal change: the ILAE documented level of certainty.

Post-traumatic stress disorder after witnessing a fatal accident, with nightmares and flashbacks, is the comorbidity that treatment targets; he does not attribute the symptoms to stress, and the diagnosis does not require him to.
Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for functional seizures; his as-needed lorazepam should not be used to abort the events (AAN 2025).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree family history of epilepsy does not make his events epileptic; the habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change answer the question.
red_herrings.data_point: Maternal aunt with epilepsy diagnosed at age 30
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic cause and start antiseizure drugs before the events are recorded

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder and childhood sexual abuse
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset two weeks after witnessing a fatal pedestrian accident
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressor alone, without positive signs or typical event semiology

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The diagnosis rests on positive signs and event semiology, not on the patient's attribution; a stressor is not required, and the explanation can be given without insisting on a psychological cause.
red_herrings.data_point: He fears multiple sclerosis or epilepsy and does not believe his symptoms are related to stress
red_herrings.intended_effect: Keep investigating, or abandon the diagnosis, because he rejects a stress explanation

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility of the right leg deficit, with entrainment of the shaking during the witnessed events. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (forced eye closure, asynchronous shaking of varying frequency, side-to-side head movements, entrainment, retained responsiveness) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Sertraline with lorazepam: additive central nervous system depression; minor.
current_medications.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed for acute anxiety (about twice per week); dicyclomine 20 mg four times daily as needed
current_medications.summary: One minor interaction (sertraline with lorazepam, sedation); benzodiazepine cautions apply to lorazepam, and the antidepressant age warning applies at 22 years.
warnings: Lorazepam: sedation, tolerance and dependence; avoid using a benzodiazepine as rescue for paroxysmal events not shown to be epileptic, and after regular use taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly.
Sertraline: boxed warning for suicidal thoughts and behavior in patients under 25 years; monitor mood, particularly after dose changes.
Dicyclomine: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness), additive with sedatives.

findings.morphology: Bilateral arm shaking, asynchronous and variable in frequency, with the eyes closed and side-to-side head movements, lasting 50 s; he answered questions during the event. Movement artifact; the posterior alpha rhythm remained discernible. No evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

Whole-body shaking with the eyes closed, irregular in amplitude, lasting 2 min 10 s. Posterior alpha rhythm persisted between artifact bursts; no evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing or suppression.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Two habitual events were recorded (asynchronous arm or whole-body shaking with the eyes closed, 50 s and 2 min 10 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact during the events partially obscured the record.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

clinical_pearls: FND is the second most common reason for outpatient neurology consultation and should be diagnosed by positive signs, not by exclusion
The Hoover sign has high specificity and moderate sensitivity for functional leg weakness and should be tested in all patients presenting with lower extremity weakness
Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures account for approximately 20-30% of patients referred to epilepsy monitoring units
A shorter symptom duration before diagnosis is associated with a better prognosis, and clear communication of the diagnosis supports engagement with treatment
Psychiatric comorbidity (especially depression, anxiety, PTSD, and history of childhood trauma) is common but not universal in FND; absence of psychiatric history does not exclude the diagnosis
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The required work-up is the examination; a video-EEG can confirm the events. A normal outside CT, his fear of multiple sclerosis or epilepsy, an aunt with epilepsy and his rejection of a stress explanation invite repeat imaging and an epilepsy work-up; the main tasks are explaining the diagnosis and treating his PTSD.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Miguel Santos is a 22-year-old right-handed man who presents to the neurology service as a direct admission from his primary care physician's office for evaluation of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of whole-body shaking over the past six weeks. The patient reports that approximately eight weeks ago he witnessed a severe motor vehicle accident in which a pedestrian was struck and killed. He was deeply affected by this event and has since experienced nightmares, flashbacks, and heightened anxiety. Two weeks after the accident, he noticed that his right leg began to feel 'heavy and weak,' initially intermittent but progressively worsening to the point where he now requires a wheelchair for mobility. He describes the weakness as affecting his entire right leg from the hip downward, and he also notes decreased sensation over the right leg and right lower abdomen. He denies any back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or left-sided symptoms. Concurrently, he has developed episodes of shaking involving his arms and sometimes his whole body, occurring two to four times daily, each lasting 30 seconds to 3 minutes. During these episodes he reports being aware of his surroundings but unable to control the movements. He denies tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or post-event confusion. His boyfriend has witnessed multiple episodes and describes them as variable in intensity and pattern, noting that they sometimes occur during stressful conversations. He reports that he has never injured himself during an episode and that he can respond to questions throughout. He was seen in an outside emergency department three weeks ago where a CT head was unremarkable and he was discharged with a referral to neurology. His primary care physician, noting the progressive nature and functional impairment, arranged for direct inpatient admission for comprehensive evaluation. The patient is worried that he may have multiple sclerosis or epilepsy and is seeking answers. He acknowledges significant psychological distress since the accident but does not believe his symptoms are related to stress.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, two brief episodes of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 45 seconds and 30 seconds were witnessed. During these events, the patient's eyes were tightly closed (forced eye closure with resistance to passive opening), the arm shaking was asynchronous and irregular, with side-to-side head movements, and varied in frequency (2-6 Hz) and amplitude. The shaking entrained to a rhythm he was asked to tap with his left foot. He remained responsive to verbal commands throughout, stating 'I can't stop it.' No post-event confusion.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing performed normally on the left; on the right, patient demonstrates inconsistent performance with exaggerated swaying but no true dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam unremarkable, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient uses a wheelchair and states he cannot walk due to right leg weakness. When assisted to stand, demonstrates a dragging gait pattern with the right leg held stiffly behind. However, on observational testing when distracted, he was noted to bear full weight on the right leg momentarily while adjusting his hospital gown. No Trendelenburg sign. Romberg testing: dramatic swaying in all directions without falling, with self-correction at extreme sway angles (functional Romberg).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent, normal rate and prosody. Affect is anxious with intermittent tearfulness when discussing symptoms. Attention intact, able to recite months of the year backward. Memory 3/3 registration, 3/3 recall at 5 minutes. No evidence of cognitive impairment.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in bilateral upper extremities. Right lower extremity demonstrates give-way weakness: initial resistance followed by sudden collapse of effort in hip flexion (2/5 on initial testing, 5/5 when distracted during seated hip flexion while donning shoes). Left lower extremity strength 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities 5/5 bilaterally. Hoover sign positive on the right: voluntary right hip extension is weak (2/5) on direct testing, but involuntary right hip extension is full when he flexes the left hip against resistance. No pronator drift. No muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the entire right leg extending to the exact midline of the groin and abdomen, with a sharp demarcation at midline. This non-anatomical pattern does not follow any dermatomal or peripheral nerve distribution. Vibration sense intact at bilateral great toes, medial malleoli, and tibial tuberosities. Proprioception intact in all digits. Upper extremity sensation intact throughout.
